axioms: A specification section (e.g. 'Semantics') and an example invocation (e.g. a systemd ExecStart line) must agree; if the invocation assumes behavior the specification never describes, an implementation built from the specification alone will not support that invocation.

Two independently-scheduled processes (an on-demand script and a fixed-time timer) that both read-modify-write the same git-tracked shared state can overlap in time regardless of how unlikely that seems from typical usage patterns.

set -e-style scripts fail atomically at the first error, which prevents partial corruption but also means a failure produces silence (no commit, no push) rather than a visible alert — silence is not the same as safety if nobody is watching for it.

Claims about a remote machine's current state (a file exists, a systemd setting is enabled, a service is running) are only true as of when they were last checked; a plan's 'checked on <date>' note is a claim to re-verify, not a fact to inherit.

Preconditions gating a destructive operation (e.g. prune) are only as strong as the state they read; if that state (git HEAD vs. origin, harvest audit result) can itself be produced by an incomplete or racing prior step, the precondition can pass on stale or wrong grounds.

A network service's binding address and authentication posture are two independent security properties; specifying 'Tailscale-only' as intent doesn't guarantee the implementation as specified actually enforces it.

Ordering guarantees between tasks in a written plan (e.g. 'Task 15 runs after Task 14') don't automatically extend to automated recurring jobs introduced later (e.g. a daily timer) unless the plan explicitly reasons about how the new schedule interacts with the earlier manual sequence.
primitives: systemd unit/timer definitions and their actual argv
git push/pull race windows across two machines
network bind address vs. intended exposure
live remote-machine state (files, services, enabled flags)
failure_mode: Trusts a spec section's prose without checking whether a concrete example elsewhere in the plan (e.g. a systemd ExecStart line) actually matches what that prose would produce.
Reasons about single-run correctness and misses what happens when two scheduled/on-demand runs on different machines overlap or race.
Accepts a plan's 'checked on <date>' assertion about remote-machine state as still true without live verification.
Evaluates security/exposure intent (e.g. a comment saying 'Tailscale only') rather than the actual binding behavior the specified implementation would produce.
